links.outcome: Rate of biased outcomes in paired cases differing only in one demographic attribute
links.effect: Biased outcomes occurred in 6.9% (single-agent) vs. 6.1% (nine-agent pipeline) of paired cases, p = 0.498; no measurable difference between conditions.
links.quote: We find no measurable difference in how often biased outcomes occur between the two conditions (6.9% vs. 6.1%, p = 0.498).

links.outcome: Whether an independent audit agent detects biased outcomes, by audit capacity
links.effect: 30.0% of biased outcomes went undetected overall; 43.8% when auditor overloaded vs. 18.4% when not. Pipeline did not reduce bias occurrence.
links.quote: We do find a large and significant effect of audit capacity on whether bias is caught: 30.0% of biased outcomes go entirely undetected, rising to 43.8% when the auditor is overloaded and falling to 18.4% when it is not.

links.outcome: Audit coverage under capacity constraint with risk-ordered queue vs first-come-first-served
links.effect: Risk-ordered audit queue raised coverage from 65.6% to 91.7% (p = 0.028) under the same capacity constraint.
links.quote: A follow-up experiment shows that reordering the audit queue by estimated risk, rather than first-come-first-served, recovers most of the lost coverage under the same capacity constraint (65.6% to 91.7%, p = 0.028).

links.outcome: Proportion of cases reviewed by auditor under load
links.effect: Coverage fell from 100.0% to 65.6% under load (p < 0.001), so unreviewed cases' biased outcomes went undetected; judgment on reviewed cases 81.6% vs 85.7%.
links.quote: Decomposing this effect shows it is driven almost entirely by coverage (whether a case is reviewed at all, which collapses from 100.0% to 65.6% under load, p < 0.001) rather than by degraded judgment on the cases that are reviewed (81.6% vs. 85.7%, p = 1.000, direction reversed).
